idea: “Given that” shrinks the group you choose from. Find the row or column for the condition, then take the part of it that has the other trait. With percents, picture a concrete total like 1,000 and build the counts.
trap: Dividing by the grand total instead of the total for the condition, or reversing the condition.
desmos: No graphing here: the work is picking the right denominator.

items.stem:
A survey asked students whether they prefer reading print books or e-books.

Of the juniors, 35 prefer print and 37 prefer e-books. Of the seniors, 40 prefer print and 8 prefer e-books.

If a student who prefers print is chosen at random, what is the probability that the student is a senior?
items.explain: The condition is “prefers print”: 35+40=75 students. Of them, 40 are seniors, so the probability is 7540​=158​.

items.stem: In a group of 180 people, 72 have a library card, and 7 of the people with a library card also have a museum pass. In all, 102 people in the group have a museum pass. If a person who does not have a library card is chosen at random, what is the probability that the person has a museum pass?
items.explain: People without a library card: 180−72=108. Museum-pass holders without a library card: 102−7=95. The probability is 10895​.

items.explain: Picture 1,000 phones: 700 from X, of which 7 are defective, and 300 from Y, of which 15 are defective. Of the 22 defective phones, 7 came from X, so the probability is 227​.
